raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with aggravated bloody stool and diarrhea for 2 months, accompanied with fever, left lower abdominal pain and tenesmus. Four years before admission, the patient was diagnosed with "colitis" for the similar symptoms not so serious without fever in another hospital. Although mesalazine had been prescribed, he had given up medications and follow-up visit without a doctor's recommendation before admission. Laboratory tests showed elevated C reactive protein (CRP) of 35.8 mg/L. Hemoglobin was decreased at 125g/L. Colonoscopy revealed extensive colitis, with wide mucosal defect and spontaneous bleeding in the sigmoid colon (Figure 1A). No obvious abnormality was found on chest CT (Figure 1B). Cytomegalovirus (CMV) inclusion bodies showed positivity. After intravenous ganciclovir and methylprednisolone, the symptoms did not improve. Hence, the patient was sequential to infliximab. Although the stool returned to normal with improvement of laboratory tests and lesions under colonoscopy (Figure 1C) after infliximab treatment for 4 times, the patient still had a fever (the temperature is about 38 C), with no other respiratory symptoms. A recheck of the chest CT showed a mass shadow right lower lung lobe (Figure 1D). After antibiotic was administrated according to the drug sensitivity results of sputum culture (which showed Acinetobacter baumannii was positive), the patient no longer had a fever, but there was no change in lung mass. What is the diagnosis? 
The colon lesions were diagnosed as ulcerative colitis (UC). Puncture and biopsy of the lung mass guided by B-ultrasound revealed granulomatous inflammation and necrosis, with multiple variable-sized encapsulated yeast cells present in hematoxylin and eosin staining, hexamine silver staining and periodic acid-Schiff staining (Figure 2A-C), the final diagnosis is Cryptococcus neoformans pneumonia. After the diagnosis was confirmed, antifungal treatment with voriconazole (0.2g oral bid) was given. Medicine for UC was changed to vedolizumab, and the patient had no bloody stool, with the ESR and CRP normalized. After vedolizumab treatment for 3 times, reexamined colonoscopy showed a slight pseudomembranous colitis in rectum sigmoid colon (Figure 2D), followed by positive results of fecal Clostridium difficile toxin test. The patient then received oral vancomycin for 14 days. After 3 months of treatment with voriconazole, the lung lesions were mostly absorbed (Figure 2E). At present, the patient continues to take voriconazole orally and receive vedolizumab treatment according to the course of treatment. There is no cough, expectoration, fever, bloody stool or diarrhea.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old male presented with aggravated bloody stool and diarrhea for 2 months, accompanied by fever, left lower abdominal pain, and tenesmus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed worsening bloody diarrhea over 2 months associated with fever, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and tenesmus. Four years prior, he had been diagnosed with colitis at another hospital for milder similar symptoms without fever and was prescribed mesalazine, which he self-discontinued along with follow-up prior to admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of colitis diagnosed 4 years prior to admission; non-adherent to prescribed mesalazine and follow-up.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bloody stool, diarrhea, fever, left lower abdominal pain, and tenesmus; later persistent fever (~38 °C) without cough or expectoration. Prior medication: mesalazine (discontinued).

objective.routine_investigations: Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) 35.8 mg/L, decreased hemoglobin 125 g/L. Later sputum culture positive for Acinetobacter baumannii; subsequent fecal Clostridioides difficile toxin test positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission colonoscopy revealed extensive colitis with wide mucosal defects and spontaneous bleeding in the sigmoid colon, positive for CMV inclusion bodies. Admission chest CT showed no obvious abnormality. Repeat colonoscopy after 4 doses of infliximab showed mucosal improvement; subsequent repeat chest CT revealed a right lower lung lobe mass shadow. B-ultrasound-guided percutaneous lung mass biopsy demonstrated granulomatous inflammation and necrosis with variable-sized encapsulated yeast cells on H&E, hexamine silver, and PAS staining. Later surveillance colonoscopy after 3 doses of vedolizumab showed mild pseudomembranous colitis in the rectosigmoid colon.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with severe ulcerative colitis (UC) complicated by colonic cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (confirmed by positive CMV inclusion bodies on colonic biopsy), followed by hospital-acquired Acinetobacter baumannii sputum infection, secondary pulmonary Cryptococcus neoformans pneumonia (confirmed by encapsulated yeast cells on H&E, hexamine silver, and PAS stains of ultrasound-guided lung biopsy), and subsequent Clostridioides difficile pseudomembranous colitis (confirmed by positive fecal C. difficile toxin test). Initial treatment with IV ganciclovir and methylprednisolone did not resolve colitis symptoms; sequential infliximab (4 infusions) normalized stools and improved colonic lesions. Fever resolved after targeted antibiotics for A. baumannii, and pulmonary cryptococcosis was treated with oral voriconazole (0.2 g twice daily) while switching UC maintenance from infliximab to vedolizumab. Intercurrent C. difficile colitis after 3 doses of vedolizumab resolved with oral vancomycin for 14 days. After 3 months of voriconazole, lung lesions were mostly absorbed, and the patient remained asymptomatic on ongoing oral voriconazole and vedolizumab with normalized ESR and CRP.
